So the first API was Android one, then API level two stood for Android 1.1, and it went all the way up to now where it is at API level 34, which is Android 14. So basically every single new official Android version that comes out gets its own API number. So you can see API 21 is Android 5.0, API 22 is 5.1, and so forth. And we're using API 24 as the minimum SDK. So software development Kit, which includes a bunch of features that we use for building applications. So you can see we can go all the way up to API 34, which is the latest Android 14 version. ### Day 1 - Understanding Gradle

Imagine you want to build a cool toy to show to your friends, and it could very well be an Android application, right? So you have a special workshop called Android Studio where you can design and create this cool toy. But before you can build, you need some parts like wheels, batteries, and so forth. In our case, it could very well be your user interface consisting of buttons, text fields, images, and so forth. And this workshop has a magical list. It's called Build.gradle, where you write down what you need and it gets them for you. And then once you have all of these parts, the workshops Magic Helper, which is Gradle, puts them together to create your toy. Before you can play with your toy, you want to make sure it works well. The magic helper checks it for you. So once everything looks good, the toy is all set. The toy is ready for you to play with, so your application is ready for you to use it or show to your friends and let them use it as well. So that's a general overview of what the Gradle does for us. It's going to be something we will look into a lot, a lot later in the course. ### Day 2 - Overview of what variables are

All right let's look over variables. So encoding a variable can be thought of as a container or a storage box where you can save data to be used later on in your program. So just like in math where variables might represent numbers, encoding variables can represent a multitude of data types. And we're going to look at data types in the next video. So generally speaking you have numbers. You have text strings. You have lists or even more complex structures which we will see even later on in the course. So when you create a variable, you're telling the computer, or in our case, the phone, to reserve a specific amount of memory space for that variable based on the data type you've chosen for it. So some data types need more storage, others need less storage. And that's something that is automatically taken care of by Kotlin for us. So how much space it's going to require and take. And that is something that we can manually override. But generally speaking most of the time it will be good enough for us not to having to do that. And once a variable is created, you can assign a value to it, you can retrieve its value, or you can change its value as needed throughout the lifespan of your program. So that means the variable only exists during the time that your app is open. So once your app is closed. Then the variable has no value anymore. So it's gone basically. All right. Variables have names which should be descriptive enough to give an idea about the data it holds. So for example, if you have a piece of data that is going to be storing a name, then the variable name should also have name somewhere in there. So for example if it's animal names then you would call the variable animal name just as an example okay. So it should be descriptive enough so that you have an idea about the data it holds. So naming is really crucial because it allows coders to reference the stored data easily. So you can just get that data from the storage and use it every single time. Now when you're manually coding everything yourself, that's probably just going to be fine enough to always enter the value yourself. But once you have more complex applications where, for example, the variable is generated based on certain conditions, then you don't know what the value of that variable will be. And that's why it's really important to have a variable that is stored somewhere. And you can call it by name and then reuse its value, so to speak, inside of your further code. Okay. And for instance, a variable named user age might hold the age of a user, while user name might hold the user's name. And these are two different data types which we're going to look at in the next video. So to summarize, variables are like containers or storage boxes. They can hold various types of data. They have names to be easily identified and accessed in the code. And their values can be set, retrieved or changed as needed. So you see here this composable that allows us to use the composable keyword and basically say whatever comes next is or should be rendered as a user interface element. So let me quickly say that out a little better. So, so basically it tells the compiler to treat a function in a declarative way, signals the compose framework that this UI is intended to define a part of a user interface to enable composition and recomposition, which basically means displaying and redisplaying or like recalculating how it should be displayed where applicable. These are basically the development approaches that Jetpack Compose takes in rendering a user interface. So that's just a different way of displaying the, well, user interface elements in comparison to XML, which we haven't touched, but you will see later on. So identify a function as Composables when marked with the composable keyword, as you can see here. And the add keyword needs to be preceding the composable keyword. Otherwise it just doesn't understand what this composable is supposed to be. So you need to have this add. And this allows composition by simplifying complex UI structures. It enables declarative UI, which takes care of rendering and updating the UI. When its state and data changes. So what the heck is that? Well, the thing is, we're going to look at state and data later on. But the thing is that data is constantly influencing our user interface. So when the data changes, we also want our user interface to change. And when our user interface does something to the data, then we want the data to change and also the user interface to change, which basically means we need to make sure that it refreshes the screen when something changes. ### Day 5 - Spacer vs Padding

Welcome back. In this video we're going to look at padding versus spacer elements in order to space our user interface accordingly. Because you can see it doesn't look too great I'd say that's because everything is so clamped together very close together. So we're going to look at the patter padding modifier and the spacer element. So the elements in our case don't have any spaces between each other and Jetpack Compose. When you want to add spaces between elements there are two primary ways. One is padding or the padding modifier, or introducing a spacer element. So an element that just spaces the thing. So what are the pros and cons of each? Well, the pros of using a padding modifier is the simplicity. So you just add a padding around your element with the padding modifier. And it's straightforward and quick, and you can apply it directly to the composable you want to space. So in example two our buttons we want to add some some padding. We can directly do that. The cons are that there is a limited reusability. So if you want to consistent spacing between multiple elements you need to apply the modifier individually every single time. So each button needs to have this padding. Each unit converter like each element would need this padding manually okay. Then there is a spacer element. So the beauty about the spacer element is the fact that it or the pro is the reusability. So the spacer element can be used to create consistent spacing between multiple elements without applying the modifier to each one separately. And it's clear intent. So using a spacer explicitly communicates your design intention, making your layout more self-explanatory. The cons, however, are. It's slightly more complex. It involves adding an additional composable to your layout, which may slightly increase code verbosity. So yeah, which one to choose? Well, the choice between using the padding modifier and the spacer element depends on your specific use case and design preferences. If you need fine grained control or only want spacing around a particular element, the padding modifier is convenient. If you want consistent spacing between multiple elements. The spacer element offers a cleaner, more reusable solution. So that being said, let's take the spacer option. We will add one underneath our text here. So we have our column unit converter. Then we have the text. And before the outlined text field that's where I'm going to use the spacer okay. So there's this composable that's called the spacer. And you need to pass a modifier. Others have a DPI of 300. Others have like even less DPI. So older devices for example, usually are not that pixel dense. And that means that the same amount of pixels span over a bigger distance. So that means that UI items wouldn't be as aligned if you would just use pixels. But if you use density pixels, then suddenly items can be aligned okay, because they basically say, okay, you have this much space on your screen and take away or use this much space. So it's like it's like 16, 16 pixels, but. Really on the screen if you have a very high density pixel screen. ### Day 6 - State - Recomposition - Remember and MutableState

Imagine you're the captain of a ship, steering it through turbulent waters. Your ship, state or current condition is vital for making decisions. This is where state management comes into play. Your crew members act as events, signaling you with crucial information. When they spot a storm, they shout Captain Storm ahead! This event triggers you to adjust your course, reflecting a change in the ship's state. Now consider you've just received a message that an island with hidden treasure is nearby. The event of exciting news leads to a change in your state as you navigate towards the treasure's location. State management and events work together seamlessly, just like a ship's captain and the crew, ensuring your journey or application progresses smoothly. In the world of Jetpack Compose, think of state management as a compass guiding your app's direction when events occur, like user actions or data updates. They act as signals for you to adjust the app state, just like a captain steering a ship in response to changing conditions. In essence, state management and events work together to keep your app on a smooth course through the dynamic landscape of user interactions, making Jetpack Compose your trusted partner for a successful journey. There are two concepts that are essential in maintaining and updating the state of your composable. The remember function and the mutable state property delegate. The remember function is used to create a persistent and remembered state in Jetpack Compose. It allows a composable to maintain its state across recompositions, even when the composable is recreated, which means the screen is refreshed, which happens a lot every single second. This is crucial for preventing data and UI states during the life cycles of your app. Recomposition is the process of regenerating and updating the UI to reflect changes in the application state or user interactions. In Jetpack Compose, your UI is represented as a tree of Composables and recomposition is how compose updates this tree efficiently when underlying data or conditions change. The mutable state property delegate is used to create a mutable state that can be updated. It's often used in conjunction with remember to manage changing data. So remember a mutable state works together where the first creates a state that persists across recompositions, ensuring that data is retained even when the composable is rerendered, where the latter enables you to update the state value when you change the value. It triggers recomposition of the composable, reflecting the updated state in your UI. So the important keywords that we need to remember are remember and mutable state. And we are going to use those inside of our application in the next video, where we're going to basically create a bunch of variables for each of the states that we want to remember, and then we can update our user interface based on how those are changing. So let's get started in the next video.

Well that means that here in our line here where it says treasures found, we don't need to add this dot value anymore because treasures found now holds the value itself. So instead of having to access the dot value, we can get the value straight away because treasures found is the value. Okay, so that's what this by keyword does for us. So you could imagine it the following way. So without the by keyword. So as we have it with this equal sign, think of treasures found as a treasure chest mutable state. And now to see the gold inside of that treasure. So the actual value you need to open the chest. So you would need to use treasure found dot value like we have here dot value. ### Day 7 - Lucy's Infinite Bookshelf and Jamies LazyColumn

All right. So in order to understand Lazycolumn, let's quickly look at an example or a little story of Lucy and her infinite bookshelf. So in the heart of a bustling city, there was a magical bookstore owned by Lucy. Lucy's bookstore was famous not just for its vast collection of books, but for its unique bookshelf known as the Infinite Bookshelf. People from far and wide came to see this bookshelf. At first glance, it looked like an ordinary shelf with a few books displayed. But as visitors started scrolling through the books, they realized that the shelf seemed to go on forever, revealing more and more books. The secret. The Infinite Bookshelf only showed the books that were in the viewer's immediate sight. As visitors scrolled, new books appeared while the ones out of view magically disappeared, ensuring the shelf was never overcrowded and always ran smoothly. One day, a curious young coder named Jamie visited Lucy's store, amazed by the infinite bookshelf. Jamie exclaimed, this is just like the lazy column in Jetpack Compose for Android app development. Lucy, intrigued, asked Jamie to explain. Jamie replied, and Jetpack Compose Lazy Column is a magical tool that allows developers to display long lists without overwhelming the system, just like your bookshelf. It only renders the items visible on the screen as users scroll. New items are composed and off screen items are discarded, ensuring optimal performance. Lucy smiled, realizing that her infinite bookshelf and lazy column shared the same magic. Efficiently displaying an endless list without a hitch. So I hope you enjoyed this story. And this is just to give you a general idea of what a lazy column is, because we're going to use lazy column as our list composable so that we can display list items, but we can also display an infinite amount of list items. So you know that you've seen that whenever you use any kind of social media application where you're scrolling and scrolling and scrolling and it never stops, right? And if you were to store all the items that were ever displayed while scrolling, then you would run out of memory very fast. And that is avoided by using lazy columns. Okay, so lazy column is basically only loading as much as it needs to be seen. That's why it's called lazy. So it's a column composable, like the ones that we have used so far, where we can use items to put them on top of each other, but it's lazy, so it's only displaying the amount that it needs to display, and all the others that disregards or discards even. Okay, so that's what we're going to use. So let's get started in the next video.

### Day 7 - let and nullable

Ella and the glimmering orb in the verdant town of Sefton, there was a young mage named Ella who possessed a glimmering orb. This orb was not just a decorative piece. It had a unique power. Whenever Ella whispered a secret into the orb, it would encase the secret in a shimmering bubble, allowing Ella to transform or use that secret safely without affecting anything outside the bubble. One day, Ella found a mysterious glowing stone. Curious about its properties but not wanting to risk exposing it directly, she whispered its essence into the orb. The orb then encased the essence of the stone in a shimmering bubble, allowing Ella to safely study and transform it without altering the original stone. What is this story about? ### Day 8 - Why Interfaces

The guilds of Crawfordsville in the town of Crawfordsville. Various guilds interfaces existed, each representing a specific craft. There was the blacksmiths guild, the bakers guild, the tailors guild, and so on. Each guild had a set of standards and practices, so methods that its members classes adhere to. However, some townsfolk were multi-talented. For instance, Sir Bakelite was not only a member of the bakers guild, but also the tailor skills, making him both a baker and a tailor implementing multiple interfaces. This multi guild membership allowed him to offer a diverse range of services, showcasing the power of multiple inheritances via interfaces. The guilds ensured that regardless of an individual's unique style or technique, certain quality standards and practices were maintained, symbolizing the contracts and interface enforces. So interfaces in programming, especially in object oriented programming languages like Kotlin, serve several essential purposes. Number one abstraction. So interfaces allow you to define a contract that classes can implement. This contract consists of method signatures that derived classes must provide implementations for. It abstracts the what from the how. A class can say, I promise to have this capability without immediately specifying how it achieves it. Then we have number two multiple inheritance. Most object oriented languages, including Kotlin, don't support multiple inheritance of classes due to the diamond problem and other complexities. However, a class can implement multiple interfaces, allowing you to inherit from multiple sources without the baggage that comes with class based multiple inheritance. And we have seen how multiple inheritance work. Basically with our third example with the archery and the bard. The singer, so to speak. Okay. Number three is flexibility and interchangeability. Since inheritance is focus on the what and not the how, you can have multiple classes implementing the same interface in various ways. This flexibility means that objects of these classes can be used interchangeably in contexts where only the capabilities guaranteed by the interface are relevant. Then there is number four encapsulation. So by using interfaces, you can hide the internal implementation details of a class and expose only the methods declared in the interface. This encapsulation ensures that external components interact with the object through a well-defined contract, and number five is evolution in scalability. As software grows and evolves, interfaces provide a stable contract that allows you to expand and refactor your underlying implementations without affecting classes that depend on the interface.

### Day 8 - Why MVVM and Why Repository

So now you might wonder, why should we use mVVM? Because it starts to get really complicated, and I really wanted to make sure that you get why we even do that. Because otherwise you might say, hey, I don't want to do any of that. And that's how I feel very often when I look at mVVM, mVVM, because it's just so much abstraction and so much stuff around it that you need to set up. So that abstraction is really one of the whole points why it's so good. So number one is separation of concerns. So mVVM promotes a clear separation between the user interface, the business logic and data. This ensures that each component has a distinct responsibility, making the code base organized and easier to maintain. Number two is testability. Because of this separation, you can test each component independently. For instance, you can test the ViewModel without needing to involve the user interface or the data source. Number three is reusability. Viewmodels are decoupled from the view, meaning you can reuse the same view model across different views or even across different platforms. If you're developing a multi-platform app, then there is data binding. mVVM can be paired with data binding mechanisms, allowing automatic updates between the view model and the view. This reduces boilerplate code and ensures the UI is always in sync with the data, and number five is maintainability. As your application grows, having distinct layers helps in managing the complexity. Changing the user interface won't affect the underlying business logic and vice versa. Now that's why an mVVM makes sense. Now let's look at why a repository makes sense, because we are going to while we use repositories already, and we're going to go even deeper in the next few videos. So a repository is a design pattern that acts as a clean API for data access to the rest of the application. Think of it as a mediator between different data sources such as remote APIs, local databases, and in-memory caches. The benefits of using a repository are abstraction, so it provides a higher level abstraction over raw data sources, allowing you to switch between different data sources without changing the rest of your application. So, for example, you get the data from the web. Cool. And now you don't get the data from the web anymore, but you can get it from a database, for example. Well, cool. No problem. Just plug and play. As I said earlier, then centralized data handling. So all data related operations are centralized in the repository ensuring consistency and reducing redundancy. Number three is isolation. By isolating data related code in a repository, you can easily mock data for testing, change data storage mechanisms, or add caching layers without affecting the rest of your app. And number four is flexibility. If in the future you decide to change how you fetch or store your data e.g. for example, moving from one database solution to another, or adding a cloud based backup, you only have to update the repository without touching the view model or the view. Now let's look at a simple analogy. Imagine you're a chef in a restaurant, so the view the ingredients you need for your dishes can come from various places a farm, a local market, or even your own garden. These are the different data sources. Now, instead of going directly to these places every time you cook, you have a trusted supplier, the repository, who fetches the best ingredients for you. The supplier knows where to get each ingredient, when to harvest them, and how to store them all. You the chef. The view care about is receiving the right ingredients for your dish. The supplier abstracts away the complexity of sourcing ingredients, allowing you to focus on cooking. Similarly, in app development, the repository handles the complexity of data sourcing, letting the view model and the view focus on their primary responsibilities. So mVVM repositories patterns might seem complex initially, but they offer long terme benefits, especially for larger applications. Their structured approach aids in managing complexity, ensuring scalability and improving maintainability. So I understand that this is a little much maybe at a given point in the course, but it's important for you to understand, which is why we're doing it, because we need to set it up so that it will be available inside of the main activity, so that we can actually run our application again.

### Day 9 - The Scroll of DataVille - JSON Analogy

The scroll of data will in the kingdom of data will, there existed a vast library. The Grand librarian. The librarian housed scrolls upon scrolls of valuable information. These scrolls were written in different languages, used various symbols, and followed unique formats. While the knowledge contained within these scrolls was immense, diversity in formats made it challenging for scholars. For scholars from neighboring kingdoms to understand and decipher them. One day, a wise mage named Jackson visited Déterville. He noticed the scholars struggles in the Librarium, and decided to introduce a universal format that would simplify the exchange of information across kingdoms. This format was named Jason Jackson's Scroll of Notation. Jason had the following magical properties. Number one simplicity. Jason was easy to read and write. It used familiar symbols like curly braces for objects and square brackets for lists. Number two universality. Regardless of the original scrolls format, it could be transcribed into Jason, ensuring that anyone, anywhere could understand the content without needing a special translator. Number three. Compactness. Jason eliminated unnecessary details, making the scrolls lighter and easier to carry. And number four hierarchy. It allowed scribes to easily represent complex relationships and hierarchies using nested objects and lists. The scholars of Déterville were thrilled. They quickly adopted Jason and began transcribing their scrolls into this new format. Word spread, and soon kingdoms far and wide began using Jason to exchange information from trade agreements to magical recipes. Thanks to Jason, the flow of knowledge became smoother. Trade flourished. Collaborations increased, and the era of the Unified Scrolls began.

### Day 9-Using Retrofit, the Suspend Key and Coroutines to get Access to Categories

The tale of the time stopping spell in the magical world of Kotlin, wizards and witches often found themselves performing tasks that took a long time, like brewing a potion or summoning a creature while waiting for one task to complete. They wished they could pause and perform other tasks without any delay. This is where the suspend spell came into play. The suspend keyword is akin to a time stopping spell. When invoked, it allows the caster so the function to pause its execution without blocking the entire magical ritual thread. So the main thread the UI thread. Once the long task is complete, the function can resume from where it left off. So in technical terms, non-blocking a suspend function doesn't block the thread it's running on, but instead it suspends the coroutines execution. When the result is ready, the coroutine resumes the coroutine context. So a suspend function can only be invoked from a coroutine or another suspend function. They are the heart of Kotlin's approach to asynchronous programming flexibility. While paused, the other tasks or functions can run, making better use of resources and improving responsiveness, especially in applications with a user interface. Okay, so this was just a little story. Now let's get back to our project and see how we can put those concepts into our app. Therefore, I will create a new file once again. For now, we just have two screens, right? We have the recipe screen and and the detail screen. So we have seen how routes work in our other project where we just would use route keywords and we would potentially run into errors. But what I want to have is I want to access my screens myself inside of the composable that will take care of navigation. So what I can do here is I can use the sealed keyword, so it is used when it is known in advance that a type will conform to one of the subclass types. So sealed classes ensure type safety by restricting types to be matched at compile time rather than runtime, so that means they will be matched already in the IDE. So inside of Android Studio, and not just after once we actually run the application. So this can make sure that we don't run into the problem where for example, we accidentally write the route name incorrectly when we want to call the route or pass the route or something like that. And that's what we make this sealed class screen for, because what I want to have is I want to have the different routes directly in here. So we pass the route of type string in here. And what I'm going to do is I'm going to create two objects. So one for the recipe screen which will be of type screen. And it will have a recipe screen as the root. Okay, now I'm going to do the same thing for my detail screen. So object detail screen screen. And here again the route will be detail screen. So this is just good practice to make sure that you're basically creating constant variables for each of those different screens that you have. But in our case we're going a step further and putting it as objects in using this screen class, the screen class. And we create directly objects inside of this screen class of screen class types, where we pass the recipe screen route name. And now we can use that route name later on again and again. Or basically this object again and again, which makes sure that we are using the right location. So to speak. Okay. Now let's go ahead and create a new file. And actually let's do that in the next video where we're going to set up the new file that will take care of the navigation itself.

### Day 10 - Serialization and Deserialization with Parcelable

The Kingdom of Data and the Mystical Land of Dataland. Messages were passed between towns using magical orbs called pass syllables. These orbs could contain anything from a simple note to a complex artifact, but to transport these items safely, they had to be magically transformed into a form suitable for the journey. This process was known as serialization. The town's chief magician, eyes, was an expert in this craft. With a flick of his wand, he could convert any object into a stream of magical essence, sealing it within a passable orb. However, the magic didn't end there. Once the pass syllable reached its destination, the contents had to be reverted to their original form for use. This reversal process was known as deserialization. The brilliance of Paracelsus's magic was that it ensured the integrity of the data, regardless of the journey's length or the challenges faced. The contents of the pass syllable remained unchanged and undamaged. This reliable system allowed for swift and secure exchanges between towns, strengthening the bonds of data. Land. In Kotlin, this magic is realized through the concept of pass syllables. Objects can be serialized into a format suitable for storage or transmission, and then deserialized back into the original form. And that is what we needed inside of our application. Because if we look at our category, the category is not just a string, right? And what we passed was an object from one screen to another inside of our recipe app. Okay, so here in the recipe app, you could see we tried to pass an entire category. So an entire object and in order to send objects from one screen to another, we need to serialize them. We need to make them parcels or pass syllables. So basically that's why we went ahead and said, okay, pass allies this category and make it passable. Or basically we said this category data class, its objects are pass syllable so we can serialize and deserialize them. That's basically what we wanted to achieve. Because what serialization does is it basically makes an object into a string. Okay. So the object has information about its ID, about the category name, about the image location. So category thumb about the description. All of this information is put into a format so that an object is then a string. And then when deserializing that pass a label is then reverted back into an object okay. So it's reverted back into being a category object. And this concept is really important whenever you want to pass complex data types such as classes or objects, because the the data type of a category. Has more than just one detail, right? It's not just a string. It's really a lot of different information. And that's where passable is so powerful, because it really helps us doing that with just adding this passable keyword to our category, making sure that we have this parser lies, importing parser lies, and obviously beforehand making sure that in this one here, but in this build.gradle making sure that we have this plugin installed, and by doing so, we're saving ourselves a lot of time, because otherwise we would have to do that manually and take care of all of that stuff ourselves. Inside of our recipe app. It now allowed us to store an entire object of our category type inside of the save state handle, which usually if you want to use a set key value pair, you can use generics here or like any type. ### Day 11 - Story about Context

The enchanted realm of Aptom and the magical land of Aptom. Every village represents an app, and every inhabitant of that village requires a unique form of energy to carry out their tasks. This energy is called context. The essence of context. The very foundation of Aptom the earth itself is the base context. It provides fundamental utilities and services like accessing resources, launching activities, and more. Then there are activities. So the village centers every village and Aptom has a center known as an activity. This center emanates its own variation of the energy tailored to the needs of the village's inhabitants. When an inhabitant wishes to perform a task within their village, they draw from the activities context. Then there are service outposts. Scattered around the village are outposts known as services. These outposts have their own reservoirs of context, allowing inhabitants to perform background tasks without directly tapping into the village center. And then there are broadcast receivers. The watchtowers. Towering watchtowers, known as broadcast receivers, stand tall around them. They catch energy signals from afar and possess their own context to process these signals and relay information. And now an aptom energy must flow seamlessly. However, if the context from one village seeps into another, it causes turmoil. Why is developers act as the guardians of abdomen, ensuring that context is used wisely and doesn't leak, preserving the harmony of the realm. Now, the thing that we are going to focus on for our location application for now is going to be using activities and using the activities context in our application. All right. So that's something that we will need to pass on. But we need to be wary of the context leakage. So let's see how we can use the context as well as how we can build a user interface of our application that checks the location of the user in the next video.

### Day 14 - Quick Overview Of Storage Options - Reading the book

A welcome back. In this video we're going to look over. A little bit of the book. So I'm going to read through a portion of the book. Chapter 11.5 Saving Data locally on Android. So this book was written by Loveth Nwokike and me, and we've been working on this book for quite some time. And yeah, basically I'm going to read a little bit from it. Also, the room database example that we have here is also from the book. So the wish list application and let's go through it. This will give you a little bit of an idea how to save data locally, or the reasons why room database is good. So saving data locally on Android stores data on the device itself, such as in a file or database. This can help improve the performance and reduce the need to access external data sources. Additionally, it can help make an application more secure by preventing sensitive data from being exposed over the internet. There are several ways to save data locally on an Android device. Below are the listed options and their explanation. Shared preferences is a simple key value storage system that allows you to save small amounts of primitive data such as strings, int, and booleans in a file on the device. You can use shared preferences to store user preferences, application settings, or any other small pieces of data you need to persist. Then there is internal storage is a file system specific to your app and accessible only by your app. You can use internal storage to save private files to your app, which should not be accessible to other apps or to other users. Then there is the external storage, which refers to storage that is not internal to the device, such as an SD card, a USB storage. You can use external storage to save files intended to be shared with other apps or users. And then there's SQLite and room. These are options you can use to save structured data. With a chance for manipulation. We will be learning about them in detail shortly. So now which of those options should you choose? Well, it depends on the specific needs of your app. For example, if you need to store small amount of data that do not require a structured database, you may use shared preferences. On the other hand, if you need to store structured data and perform complex queries, you may choose to use SQL or room. So why aren't we using SQL? Well, let's talk about SQL real quick here. SQL is a lightweight embedded SQL database engine that is well suited for storing and retrieving data in Android apps. You can use SQL Lite to store structured data in a database and perform queries on the data over time. It was found to be complex, requiring long lines of code for its actualization. So that's where room came in. Room was created to reduce this complexity. It's an Android library that makes it easier to work with SQL databases. So basically it's like a layer on top of SQL databases or SQL Lite databases. It provides an abstract layer over SQLite, allowing you to interact with the database using data access objects called doors. So we're going to set up a Dao in the next few videos so you can focus on building the app's features. Room introduced some key features that facilitate the integration of local database into your application. They are listed below. So it's the entity class which we'll need to set up. Well, actually we already have an entity class. In our case it's called the. Wait a second. How did we call it. We just didn't call it data class or entity class. So it's our wish okay. So we need the entity class. Then we need the Dao which is the data access object. We need basically to set up those Crud operations that I was talking about. So it's an abstract class. In this case it was a person right. So we have the insert. We have the well basically create search or read update and delete. So this query here is another way to search. So this is searching a user by its id. This one is searching a user while all users in a given database table. All right. So we're going to set all of that good stuff up in the next few videos. And then we can basically use that using a database okay. Now you see there is this class people database that inherits from room database using the person Dao. And the person Dao is in turn using well accessing these entity items such as the primary key of the person and the last. For example. Because you see, whenever you add a user, you're passing a person object. Whenever you update a user, you're also passing a person object and so forth. Then there's also something called flow. ### Day 14 - Setting up the @Entity for our Data Class Wish

Welcome back. In this video we're going to prepare our data class being or it becoming an entity so that we can actually use it with our Dao and with the room database. So it's quite simple. So you take the data class that you want as the object type that you want to store permanently on your device using the room database. In our case it was the data class wish. And you add the entity annotation to it which comes from Android Room. All right. Now you need to say in which table you want to store that information. So here I'm going to say table name. And then we need to add a string. So I'm going to call this one wish table. All right. So the database will now have a table which then contains data about our wishes. Now we will create wishes in every single wish will become a new row. And now we need to define the columns that we want to have inside of that database. Inside of that table. Okay. So you have the level of the database. In which you have tables, multiple tables. You can obviously also have just one table or no tables at all. Then the database is empty, but you can have one table and multiple tables. In our case we will have one table which will be our wish table. And then in that table you have columns which will be the different properties of your data class. And then each entry of your. Table will be a new row. So we now need to say which one of those will be the primary key. Which one of those items here will be the primary key of those properties? Okay. So now you see that this doesn't work. Why does this not work? Because we need to add something called a late init modifier to our variable. So we have not used late init before, but let's look at what it does. In this video so late in it. VAR is a promise that you make to the Kotlin compiler that the variable will be initialized before you call any operations on it. So how does that work from a flow perspective? So you have to consider that when you want to use a variable, the variable needs to exist. So when you want to access a variable inside of your code later on, the variable needs to exist, because otherwise you run into an error because basically the variable doesn't exist and you're trying to access it and that crashes your application. So if you want to create a variable that will take some time. To be created like stuff that runs with a coroutine. Right? So this whole flow thing, which works via a coroutine whenever you have something that happens asynchronously and can take a little while, like flow coroutine stuff, then you need to make sure that you add this late init, which is a late initializer. We're basically saying, hey, we promise that we're going to initialize this variable before we're going to actually use it. So. To delve deeper late in it. VAR is often used when you have some property that cannot be initialized during the object creation, but you need it to be non-null once it is initialized. A common scenario is when you're working with dependency injection frameworks like dagger, or when you're assigning values to properties after some setup method, such as in Android development where you assign values to properties after the layout has been inflated. However, there are some limitations. Latent var can only be used with mutable properties since it has to be a var, so we cannot use val, which means the property can be changed. It also can't be used with primitive types. If you try to access late init var property before it has been initialized, it will throw an uninitialized property access exception. And that was the error that was talking about earlier. So basically we're saying. We're going to set this thing up before we need it, because otherwise, if it was a simple variable that we can just set up like so. VAR my int is going to be five for example. Right. That's easy. That just happens synchronously and there's no problem with it at all. It's instantly initialized. At the moment we create the variable, we are directly initializing a value to it. But here with a flow that's not possible because it happens asynchronously. And that's why we need to make sure that we use this late init keyword. Remember, use late init when you are sure about the initialization and you want to avoid null checks every time you access the property. So an alternative would have been to constantly check hey, is this thing a null or empty or not? But flow doesn't even accept that. So basically flow just says hey, you need to use late init var, otherwise I'm not going to work. So that's step number one. Now we need to do the actual initialization. So there is this init initializer. We saw that earlier a lot earlier when we looked at classes. So we're going to say what kind of dispatcher we want to use. Now what are dispatchers. So dispatchers in Kotlin coroutines are responsible for deciding what thread or threads the coroutine will run on. There are several types of dispatchers, each designed for different kinds of operations and workloads. So in our case we're using dispatcher.io IO standing for input output. So we're basically using input to add a wish right or output to load a wish. So this one is predefined dispatcher in Kotlin that is optimized for input output related operations. This means operations that can block the thread they are running on without consuming a lot of CPU. Such operations include reading and writing to files, database operations, and network calls, which often require waiting for the data to be read or written, and during this time the thread is mostly idle. So that's what this dispatcher IO does. So it maintains a shared pool of threads that can grow or shrink according to the demand. This allows for efficient management of threads when you have many coroutines performing IO operations that are sporadically active. So by using this, you ensure by using this dispatcher IO, you ensure that the system's resources are used efficiently and you don't block the main thread, which would otherwise lead to poor application performance and a bad user experience. So in practice, when you launch a coroutine for an IO task, you would specify the dispatcher like we did right here. And this effectively tells the coroutine builder that the coroutine should run on a thread that is part of the IO dispatches thread pool. So that's pretty cool. That's just a way to make it more efficient. And so that's how to add a wish. And you know what? Let's just copy this thing and do the same thing for update wish okay. ### Day 14 - Dependency Injection

Welcome back. In this video I want to give you an idea about dependency injection. So let's start. So first off dependencies are like the rules in a board game. Just like you need to know the rules to play the game. Pieces of code need certain information or tools to do their job. Let's say you're playing a game and you need dice, but instead of looking for them yourself, there is a helper who always hands you the dice when it's your turn. That's what dependency injection does in apps. It gives the pieces of your app what they need, like the dice in the game, without them having to look for it. This means the app can run smoothly because all the parts know they will get what they need without worrying about how to find it. This helper makes sure that if part of your app needs to change, you don't have to go through the whole app looking for all the places that need that new part. Instead, your helper takes care of it for you, and that's pretty much the gist of dependency injection. It keeps things organized and makes it easier to manage changes in your app.

----------------------------------------

### Final Touches And Sending Data Via Intent - putExtra

Welcome back. In this video, we are going to finalize the application and therefore we're going to use the START activity for result functionality as well as we are going to basically send over the details from our other activities to this result activity which needs to know, first of all, what's the name of the user who won and then the score. So let's go ahead and actually build this in our project. Therefore, let's go ahead to our constants because our constants are going to contain constant variables. And whenever you send data from one activity to another, it's good to store the name under which you stored the details that you want to have in a constant. So this will make a lot more sense once we get started with it. So first of all, I'm going to call this one user underscore name and here it's common practice to use capitalized letters and use underscores when you have a name with multiple words. So here this will be of type string. And I'm going to say that the user name will be the underscore user name. So this string is how it will be stored internally, and that's the constant name that I'm using. So I'm passing the username and I'm also going to have to pass the total amount of questions. So let's create the constant value, total underscore questions, which will also be of type string and it will contain the value called total questions like so. And then I need the correct answer so I will create another const while correct answers, which will be of type string also, and it will have the string correct answers stored. So these are just going to be the keys, so to speak, and the which we are storing. So the location, so to speak, under which we are storing the details so that we can retrieve them when we are moving data from one activity to another. So let's go over to our very first activity, our main activity where we now need to send the data over. So once we click on the button and this intent starts, we are starting an activity. So now what we're going to do is we're going to start this activity, but we're also going to pass additional data. So you can do that by using put extra on an intent. So an intent can have extra information that you send over from one activity to another, and you can then retrieve the information on the other activity. So here I'm going to use this put extra method and you can see there are many different overloads, one with a name which is the key and then the value being integer by char along and so forth. So you can send over all kinds of data and here you can see what you can send over. So even c realizable and past available files, which is basically a way how you can send entire classes over. But we're going to see that only later. Now it's not necessary. So first of all, I will need to pass in a key here, which is the first entry in the put extra. So I'm going to use this constant here because it's good practice. Of course, I could have just written something like username here. That would have been fine as well as long as I know on the other side that I also need to retrieve username. But it's just good practice to use constants here because if I use hardcoded strings I might run into errors. So here I will pass over their name. And where do I get it from? Toast. You might wonder. All right, let's look at it. It also was available right from the start. Snack bars were only added in the API level 23. The activity is not required to be shown in Android when you want to run a toast. So what can happen is you run it toast. The activities closed and toast still persists. All right. In snack bars, that's not the case. So the snack bar will only be visible in the activity of the application. It can't be. Or the host can't perform an action based on user input. In the snack bar, you can set something up. So if the user clicks on the snack bar, then you can run some additional code. The task cannot be dismissed by swiping well. The snack bar can and toes cannot handle user input like a swipe, etc. and snack bar can. And the toast is good for showing info messages to user and the snack bar is good for showing warning info type messages to user that need attention. So you can learn more about it here on this StackOverflow post, you can just Google Android snack bar versus toes. You can find some more information about that here. All right. ### Do something in the Background using Coroutines

In this video, you are going to learn how to use code routines. And why do we need code routines? Well, in Android. Some operations or tasks take a longer time to complete, and these tasks block the user interface. And until they are completed, the user interface is not interacted with. So the user cannot interact with it, or at least with parts of the application, and which will make the user idle and will make them bored and so forth. So it's not a good process, it's not a good approach, basically. So to avoid this Android UI system was built to only accept delays of maximum 5 seconds. So let's look at that. So I have this little application here and once I click on this button, there will be a very long lasting task running and let's just run it. You see, the UI is frozen. I cannot click on anything. The app is frozen basically. And after 5 seconds, Android decides, Hey, this is a bad application, it's not responding, let's close it, even though you see it's done. So even though the application did finish in the meantime, while this pop up appears so I can either close the app or I can wait and then go back to the app and it works, right? Otherwise the user would just close it because he believes the app is bad and he's going to uninstall it or she's going to uninstall it. So what is going on in this application that I've built here? But I'm doing that in the on create and I'm doing that on the main thread. So on the user interface, Fred, which really is not good and we can avoid that by using code routines which will basically push tasks that last longer into the background, onto a different thread so that the UI thread will not be blocked and can still run and will still run flawlessly and fluidly so that the user can properly use it. So let's look at what core routines are and a little presentation and see the advantages and then build a little application around it. So let's look at code routines and scopes in a little more details. So to summarize the features of core routines, first of all, they are lightweight. This means that you can run many code routines on a single thread due to the support of suspension. Then you have fewer memory leaks. By running a core routine and a specific scope, you ensure that they do not leak as it terminates at the end of its scope. Then you have built in cancellation support. So the launch option returns a job which can be used to cancel the running code routine and it is integrated into jetpack. ### Intro to RecyclerViews

Welcome back. In this video, I would like to talk about the recycled view on a theoretical level and why we use it, because we will use recycled views quite a bit and they are super important pretty much in any application because they allow us to use lists and list views and great views and those kinds of things. So let's look at it. First of all, Android used to use the list view and grid view classes for displaying lists. A recycle view can be thought of as a combination of list view and grid view, so it allows us to do both. However, in a recycle view, there are features that separate your code into maintainable components, even as they enforce memory efficient design patterns. So it's a lot more efficient. Pretty much. So it's a better way to create lists then list view and grid view ever were. And why should we use a recycle view? Well, imagine you're creating a list view with complicated custom items such as, for example, in Facebook you have images and then you have text and then you have the like button amount of likes, who posted it and so forth, all these kinds of things. They are complicated custom items, so to speak, and you create a row layout for the items and you use that layout inside your adapter. Well, you inflate your item layout and get view referencing each view with a unique ID, you provide it in XML to customize and add view logic. You pass that to the list view and it's ready to be drawn on the screen. Well, is it or is it not? Well, the thing is list using grid is only do half the job of achieving true memory efficiency. And that is something that is super important to more complicated your individual list items become of course, because then there is a lot going on and there's a lot to load. And if you have many images that need to be loaded, then well, this whole stuff has to be super efficient, otherwise it feels laggy, especially now with faster and faster screens. In terms of the frequency they display, for example, with 120 hertz, everything needs to be super fast. Another reason to use the recycle view is to recycle the item layout, but don't keep references to the layout. Children forcing you to call find by view for every child of your item layout every time you call get view. So it's not doing that. That's what list you did. All this calling around can become processor intensive, especially for complicated layouts. And furthermore, the situation can cause your list of scrolling to become jerky and non-responsive as it tries to grab you references. So it was fine back in the day, but then things got a lot more complicated. Of course, devices got faster, but still, why not improve if it's not perfect? Right? So that's what they thought when they created Recycle Use. Android initially provided a solution to this problem on the Android developer side with smooth scrolling via the power of the view holder pattern. And with this pattern, a class becomes an in-memory reference to all the views needed to fill your layout. You set the references once and reuse them. Working around the performance hit that comes with repeatedly calling this find view by ID and find you by ID is something that we've never used before because we just didn't need to do it. That's the beauty of Kotlin. They just got rid of this whole thing. You don't need to use it anymore. In Java. It's quite prominent and very important to use it. But well, in cotton it's less important and you can even reduce your code to where it's not even used at all. So it's pretty cool. Take note that this is an optional pattern for list view are great view. If you're unaware of this detail, then you may wonder why your list view and great views are so slow. Well, the thing is we never used list views. Anchorage View. So this is something that doesn't really bother us too much because we will use recycled views all the time. So we're not even going to start with doing list views and grid views. We're going to start with recycle straight away. So it's going to be a lot more efficient from the start and you will see how to build those things. All right. So the arrival of the recycler view changed everything. It still uses an adapter to act as a data source. However, you have to create view holders to keep references in memory to provide a new view. Recycle view either creates a new view holder object to inflate the layout and hold those references or it recycles one from the existing stack. So why is it called Recycle View? Well, another perk of using recycle views is that they come with default animations that you don't have to create or add yourself because it requires a view holder. The recycler view knows which animation to apply to which item and add them as required. So you can also create your own animations and apply them as needed. Now there is something called layout manager in recycled views and we're going to actually use that in order to adjust our recycle view elements. So the list items in our list. So the last and most interesting component of our recycler view is its layout manager. This object positions the recycle of use items and tells it when to recycle items that have transitioned off screen. And this is something that list views used to do by themselves back in the day. So you can imagine that when working with lists, there are multiple things which are important to consider. So one of them is, for example, when you scroll, then you want to see the next list elements directly. You don't want them to load, you don't want them to take up time in order to load whatever is displayed in them you want to see directly, it has to feel smooth and look smooth and that is something that is achieved a lot easier with a recycle abuse. Now another thing is you need, of course, to free up space, memory space of elements that are not visible anymore. So if a list item is not visible anymore, it's off screen already. Then at one point you need to release the memory and you shouldn't do that directly. Maybe the user wants to scroll back. All right, so maybe he wants to see whatever he scrolled away. So it doesn't have to be done directly, but it's something that recycle used or just recycle view class and layout manager handle themselves. So it's super powerful. So the recycle view has broken out this functionality to allow for different kinds of layouts, vertical, horizontal grid, staggered or a very custom. So that is the cool thing and super powerful. You're not limited to grid or list use, but you can really go ahead and build your own layouts and they are still going to be efficient because they will still be recycled views, right? So layout manager offers free choices by default. So the linear layout manager positions item to look like a standard list view. Then the grid layout manager positions items in a grid format similar to a grid view. And then we have the staggered grid layout manager which positions items in a staggered grid format. The cool thing is you can of course go ahead and create your own layout managers to use with a recycle view if you want some extra customization. So these are the basics of recycle use. And I found this guide here under guides dot com slash android slash using the recycler view which is pretty cool. So this guy created a great guide on recycled views, how they work and what you can do with it. And it's a super extended one. You can see there are a bunch of sections. So using recycled views, defining a model, notifying the adapter. So a lot of stuff you can see that he even goes to animators. And so this is an example of what you can do with a staggered grid layout. You can see pretty cool. Of course, it really depends on the images you have and the stuff, but in the end you can see it's neither a real grid layout nor is it a list view. It's really a staggered grid, so pretty powerful stuff. And then also when it comes to animations, as you can see, the elements, they get bigger the further they are in their loading process, so to speak. Okay, so this is just one website. Of course, there are a bunch of other great links to other websites. So this is also, for example, a grid view here that is used in the. Google play store. So they also use this effect here. And you can see you can pretty much find anything here. So I would highly recommend to check that out if you want to know more about recycle use. Of course, we're going to use recycle views and we are going to use some of the features that are explained in here, but of course, not everything. So that is something that I in general really encourage you to do. Each time that we cover something new that you should also look into other resources to get a bigger understanding of it. Because the more different examples you can see, the better your understanding of something very concept will become. Okay, so see you in the next video.

### Room Database Demo Part 1 - Introduction to Room Database

All right. So let's have a look at what we're going to build. You can see this little application here, which is called Room Demo, and it allows us to store data permanently. We're going to use room for that, which is part of Jetpack, which is a library that was introduced for Android App Development a couple of years ago and is now the best practice way of storing data. So let's try this. So let's say I have a name and an ID that I want to store in here. So Dennis ad info dot com, for example and I add this record. So now I have this record which will be there permanently. So even if I close my application and then I come back to it, the data will still be there. If I now delete this data. And I come back to the application after closing it. The data will be gone as well. So this is just a clean way of storing data permanently on your phone, which you will need for quite some different types of applications. So let's have a look at what room is and understand this a little better. So basically. Room allows us to save data in a local database. It's part of the Android Jetpack Suite, which is a suite of libraries to help developers follow best practices. And it contains a bunch of different libraries, as you see here. If you scroll through it, there are many, many, many. And we're going to specifically use room now. The Room Persistence Library provides an abstraction layer over SQLite to allow fluent database access while harnessing the full power of SQL light. In particular, room provides the following benefits you can see here compile time verification of SQL queries, convenience annotations that minimize repetitive and error prone boilerplate code and streamline database migration paths. So basically it's building up on SQL Light, which would have been the old fashioned approach of storing data permanently on your Android device. But it's basically just a layer on top which allows us developers to do it in a safer fashion and a lot more conveniently. So let's look at a little presentation here that we've prepared. So first of all, let's look at an introduction here. Basically, saving information locally on a device is a very important feature for any Android application users. Most at times would like to have their data available on the phone easily without needing to connect to the internet. And the SQLite database is provided in Android to make saving data locally possible, but it involves quite a number of boilerplate code lines. So Room is a jetpack library as we saw, which was created as a wrapper around SQL Light. It makes it easy to write complex SQL statements to query the data you need without having to go through every single column. So let's look at the components of room. So there are three components. First of all, the entity, which is a data class that serves as the database table and will contain variables to build out a column, the class must be annotated with the add entity keyword and must have a variable that will serve as primary key, which is denoted by the annotation primary key. We're going to see what that all means. It's confusing to just see a word and a bunch of sentences following it. We're going to specifically see how that is used in an actual example, as we've seen with the little room demo. So then we have the Dow and the Dow is an acronym for Data Access Object and is an interface that contains the necessary query to be performed for any of the operations required by the app. There are available convenient methods like add insert at fetch, add update, add delete and there is also a query that allows you to write custom SQL statements and also note that you must annotate the interface with at Dow and then we have the database. This class is annotated with ADD database and extends the room database. It contains the database setup with the entity and serves as the main access point to the database access point. Okay. So let's see all of this stuff in action in the next video.

### Getting The Users Location

Welcome back. The next thing that we want to do is to get the location of the user and then actually get it as a readable location. So we can, of course, get the latitude and longitude and we could populate this text field here with those two numbers. But it's not really something that the user can read, right? So it makes a lot more sense to have a readable location. And what we're going to use for this is going to be the fuse location provider. It's not going to be specifically for this, but we are also going to use the fuse location provider. And the fuse location provider allows us to get a pretty precise location of the user. And what it does is it takes advantage of signals provided by multiple sensors in the device to determine the device's location.
